function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below are the files you’ll need to add to the **nodejs‑welcome** repository, along with the exact Git commands to commit and push them.  
*(I’m assuming the app listens on port 3000 – adjust if your `package.json` uses a different port.)*

---

## 1. Dockerfile (root)

```dockerfile
# Use the official lightweight Node.js 18 image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /app

# Install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install --production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` keeps the image small.  
> * `npm install --production` installs only production deps.  
> * `EXPOSE 3000` matches the typical Express port.  

---

## 2. Kubernetes manifests (`k8s/` folder)

Create a folder named `k8s` at the repo root and add the following two files.

### 2.1 `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
```

### 2.2 `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What to replace:**  
> * `<YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>` – e.g., `docker.io/zelarhq`.  
> * If you’re using a private registry, make sure the image name includes the full path.

---

## 3. GitHub Actions workflow (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`)

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v2
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v3
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

    # Optional: Deploy to Kubernetes (requires a KUBECONFIG secret)
    # - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
    #   uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v1
    #   with:
    #     manifests: |
    #       ./k8s/deployment.yaml
    #       ./k8s/service.yaml
    #     kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
```

> **Secrets you’ll need to set in the GitHub repo settings:**
> * `DOCKER_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub (or other registry) username.  
> * `DOCKER_PASSWORD` – your Docker Hub password or personal access token.  
> * `KUBECONFIG` – optional, if you want automatic deployment to a cluster.

---

## 4. Commit & Push

Open a terminal in the repo root and run:

```bash
# Add the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# Commit with a descriptive message
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions CI"

# Push to the main branch
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger on the next commit to `main`, building the Docker image and pushing it to your registry. If you enabled the Kubernetes deployment step, it will also apply the manifests to your cluster.

---

### Quick Checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|---|------|
| ✅ | Dockerfile added |
| ✅ | `k8s/deployment.yaml` & `k8s/service.yaml` added |
| ✅ | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` added |
| ✅ | Secrets set in GitHub repo settings |
| ✅ | Files committed & pushed |

That’s it! Your Node.js app is now containerized, ready for Kubernetes, and continuously built via GitHub Actions.
